Where generative AI actually pays off in the enterprise

AIBy the OneClicq team9 November 20266 min read

Most businesses have now tried a chatbot or two. Far fewer can point to a generative AI project that saves real money every month. The gap is rarely the technology. It is usually the choice of problem.

Start with the work, not the model

Generative AI is good at a specific kind of task: reading, summarising, drafting and reformatting language at speed. It is much weaker at tasks that need guaranteed accuracy, fresh facts it has never seen, or judgement that carries legal or financial risk. The projects that pay off line up with the first list and keep a person in charge of the second.

A useful test is to look for work that is high volume, text heavy and reviewable. If your team does something hundreds of times a month, the input is mostly documents or messages, and a person can check the output in seconds, it is a strong candidate.

Five places it reliably earns its keep

1. Document intake and data extraction

Invoices, purchase orders, KYC forms, insurance claims and delivery notes arrive in every format imaginable. A language model can read them, pull out the fields you need and hand them to your ERP or CRM, with low-confidence cases sent to a person. This removes hours of manual typing without removing control.

2. Customer support drafting

Instead of answering customers directly, the model drafts a reply from your help articles and past tickets, and an agent edits and sends it. Agents handle more tickets, answers become more consistent, and nothing goes out unchecked.

3. Search across internal knowledge

Policies, SOPs, contracts and project notes are usually scattered across drives and inboxes. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets staff ask a question in plain language and get an answer with links to the source documents, so they can verify it.

4. Sales and proposal preparation

First drafts of proposals, RFP responses and follow-up emails, built from your own templates and product information, give sales teams a head start. The final wording stays with the person who owns the client relationship.

5. Code and test assistance

For software teams, AI assistants speed up boilerplate, test writing and documentation. The gain is real but modest, and it depends on strong code review.

Where to be careful

  • Unchecked customer-facing answers. A model can state wrong information with confidence. Anything that reaches customers without review needs tight limits on what it may say.
  • Sensitive data. Decide what data may leave your systems, choose providers and settings that do not train on your inputs, and log what is sent.
  • Decisions with legal weight. Credit, hiring, medical or legal decisions need human judgement and an audit trail, with AI as an assistant at most.

How to choose and measure your first project

  1. Pick one workflow with a clear owner, a measurable volume and an existing manual cost.
  2. Measure the baseline: time per item, error rate and backlog, before you build anything.
  3. Build a narrow pilot with a person reviewing every output for the first few weeks.
  4. Compare against the baseline, including the time spent reviewing, not just the time saved.
  5. Scale only what works, and reduce review gradually where accuracy proves itself.

A focused pilot like this usually takes weeks, not months, and gives you a real number to take to the board instead of a demo.

The takeaway

Generative AI pays off when it removes repetitive language work from skilled people and leaves them to check, decide and handle exceptions. Start small, measure honestly and keep people in the loop where mistakes are costly.
